title: Reconcile first
hook: leave your gift at the altar and first be reconciled (Matthew 5:23–24)
tomorrow: why would anyone carry a stranger's load twice as far?

segments.voice: Yesterday: salt and light, good works seen so the praise goes past you. Today the sermon stops a man in the middle of worship.

Candle lit, song started, a quiet minute finally found, and a name drops in: a friend who got snapped at last week. That's yesterday's question. What do you do with it, right there? Jesus answers with a scene, in the same sermon on the hill. Nobody in it is a villain. A man has brought his offering all the way to the altar. The gift is in his hands. And in that moment, he remembers.
screen: `A QUIET MINUTE, AND A NAME.` → `THE GIFT AT THE ALTAR.` → `HE REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Here are the words. "Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Notice two things. The worship is already under way, and Jesus says stop: put the gift down, go. And notice who's upset. Not "if you have something against him", but if your brother has something against you. The repair is yours to start. That's the teaching: in Christian life, peace with a person comes before the offering to God. In the Catholic Mass, the sign of peace comes before communion, and some readers link it to this verse. Now the neighbor who shares it. The Mishnah, a foundational collection of Jewish law, teaches that on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, wrongs between a person and God are atoned. But wrongs between a person and another person are not atoned until he has made peace with the one he wronged. Same order: the person first. And an honest difference. In the Mishnah, this teaching sits inside a holy day each year and a whole practice of asking forgiveness. In Matthew, it interrupts any offering on any day: leave it there, and go now. What the two share is a refusal of the shortcut: no settling things with God while a person is still waiting on you.

segments.voice: Open your messages and find one person things are a little off with. Write one honest line of peace, no defense and no "but". Send it if it's ready; if it isn't, keep the draft and sit quietly with their name.
Reconcile first: put the gift down, make peace with the one who has something against you, then come back and offer it.
Hold on to this: reconcile first, and the gift will keep. Two days into the sermon.

howItsDone: Christians read Matthew 5:23–24 as putting peace with others before worship; in the Catholic Mass the sign of peace comes before communion. In Jewish practice, people ask forgiveness of those they've wronged before Yom Kippur, following Mishnah Yoma 8:9.
